Impossible Travel — a guided SOC investigation
  1 / 1
Start●

An alert fired overnight. Work out what actually happened.

no experience neededabout 80 min

Somebody tripped a security alert overnight. Your job is to decide one thing: is this a real attack that must be escalated, or a false alarm that can be closed?

The alert is real and waiting for you: the setup file installs a detection rule and does not finish until that rule has actually fired, so when your browser opens you are looking at the genuine Security → Alerts page with three critical alerts on it. Card 5 walks you through it before you type anything.

You will answer it the way a real analyst does — not by guessing, but by following the evidence from the very first search to the last and writing down what you find as you go. By the last card you will know exactly which account was used, from where, how fast, and what left the building afterwards.

What this guide is

It starts at zeroNo security knowledge, no Elastic experience, no typing. If you can double-click a file, you can do this lab.
It shows every screenEvery picture is a real screenshot of a real Elastic Stack running this exact lab, with numbered circles telling you what to look at.
It never leaves you guessingEvery step says what to do, what you should see, and why it matters. If a step is a dead end, the card says so.
It cleans up after itselfOne file starts the lab — setup-lab.cmd on Windows, setup-lab.sh on macOS or Linux. One file removes it completely. Nothing is left behind.

How to move around

This guide is a deck of cards, one step each. Move through it however you like:

  • The Next and Back buttons at the bottom, or the arrow keys on your keyboard.
  • The row of pills under the header jumps you straight to any step.
  • On a phone, swipe left and right.
  • Press ? any time for help, or the printer icon to save the whole thing as a PDF.
  • On the Write it up card, type your report into the boxes and press EXPORT MY SUBMISSION to get it back as a PDF file.
  • Click any picture to open it full size. The screenshots are 1680 pixels wide, so the small print is small on purpose — one click fixes that.
Two honest notes, before you start

1. The pictures are photographs, not drawings. Every screen in this guide was captured from the running Elastic Stack 9.1.0 with this lab loaded, so every word, number, button and tab is the genuine label on your screen too. They are cropped regions of a 1680×1000 window, which is why the proportions look wide.

2. Values the pictures deliberately cover up are marked in yellow like this. Finding those is the actual exercise. Nothing in this guide is filled in for you and there is no answer key inside it — every figure you need, you read off your own screen and write in yourself.

The one thing you need first

Docker, installed and running — Docker Desktop on Windows or macOS, Docker Engine on Linux. That is the only prerequisite. The lab runs inside it and installs nothing else on your computer. If you do not have Docker yet, ask your instructor — this lab assumes it is already there.

Prep1

The words you need to know

read once

You will see all of these in the tool and in your report. Read them once now and the rest of the lab becomes much easier.

The pieces

AlertA rule that fires when something looks dangerous. It is a hint, not a fact. Your job is to confirm or dismiss it.
ElasticsearchThe database that stores and searches the logs. Answers at 127.0.0.1:9200.
KibanaThe website you do all the work in, sitting on top of Elasticsearch. Lives at 127.0.0.1:5601.
IndexOne named pile of log records of the same shape. Ours are auth-* and network-*.
Data viewKibana’s word for “which pile shall I look at”. Older versions called it an index pattern.
DocumentOne single log record. There are 294 in the auth pile and 126 in network. This is what you read.
FieldOne labelled box inside a document, like source.ip. The part before the dot is the group.
TimestampThe @timestamp field — when it happened. Every time in this lab is stored in UTC.
QueryA typed question, like “show me events where the code is 4625”.
KQLThe query language Kibana speaks. You type it in the wide box at the top of Discover.
DiscoverThe Kibana screen you will use for the whole investigation: a query box on top, results underneath.
IOCIndicator of Compromise — a piece of evidence that something bad happened, e.g. an IP address or a machine name.

The two verdicts you will have to choose between

True positiveThe attack is real. Escalate it, contain it, tell someone.
False positiveNothing bad happened. Close the alert with a note saying why not.

The pattern in the alert

Internal addressAnything starting 10.0.4. is inside your own network. Three workstations in this lab use that range, and you will meet their addresses in the results.
External addressAnything else is out on the internet. The ranges 192.0.2.x, 198.51.100.x and 203.0.113.x are the ones you will meet.
Impossible travelOne account signs in successfully from two or more places so far apart, so fast, that the same person could not have travelled between them. A classic sign of stolen or shared credentials.
Lateral movementAn attacker who is already inside hopping from one machine to another. you will not find any here — and card 17 explains why that matters.

The three fields that matter most

Almost every question in this investigation is answered by three fields. Learn these and you can read anything in the lab:

  • user.name — which account. The alert names one, and it is jdoe.
  • event.code — the number of the Windows log record; it tells you what kind of thing happened. You only need three:
    4624 = logon succeeded  ·  4625 = logon failed  ·  4688 = a program was started
  • source.ip — the address the connection came from. destination.ip is the address it went to.
The shape of the attack, before you see it

Impossible-travel attacks look like this: one account, several successful logons, each from a different external address, inside a window far too short to cross on foot — and often a large outbound transfer afterwards. Hold that shape in your head. Two of the three most obvious searches in this lab are dead ends, and the card that says so is as important as the one that finds the answer.

Prep2

Four questions you have to answer

the goal

The alert does not tell you what happened. It tells you to look. These are the four questions your report must answer, and each one has a query in this guide that answers it.

What you must find, and where it comes from
QuestionAnswered on card
1. How many successful logons did the alerted account make?Query 4 — card 13
2. From how many different external addresses did they come?Query 5 — card 14
3. How much time passed between the first and the last one?Query 7 — card 16
4. Did a large amount of data leave the network afterwards, and to where?Query 8 — card 17
Keep this sheet open

Write your answers on paper or in a text file as you go, not at the end. The four values you are looking for are marked in yellow wherever this guide mentions them — that is your reminder to go and read the value off your own screen.

There is no trick question here

Every count this guide quotes is re-measured from the running index by the setup file every single time it runs, and it refuses to finish if one of them disagrees. So if your screen says something different, one of three things is true: you are on a different data view, a different time range, or your copy of the data is not the one this guide was written against. Card 21 lists how to tell which.

One file starts the lab

first run is slowthen wait

The lab is a real Elastic Stack running on your own computer, hidden behind one file that does all the work. You start it once; it loads everything for you.

Do this

  1. Open the lab folder — the folder that contains this file.
  2. Find the file called setup-lab.cmd.
  3. On Windows, double-click it. A black command window opens, works through ten numbered stages and waits for Kibana to start. Do not close it.
  4. On macOS or Linux, open a terminal in that same folder and run ./setup-lab.sh. If your system says permission denied, run bash setup-lab.sh instead — that always works. To see what the file can do, run it with --help.
  5. Wait until it prints The lab is ready. and the two addresses. This is the slow part: a few minutes the very first time while it downloads two large images, seconds afterwards.
  6. Your web browser opens by itself at the end, on the Security → Alerts page, and asks you to sign in once. That is the next card.
The one thing that stops most people

Docker must be installed and running. The lab runs both programs inside Docker containers — Docker Desktop on Windows or macOS, Docker Engine on Linux. If the setup file says docker was not found, or that it is installed but not responding, start Docker, wait until it says it is running, then run the file again. That one check fixes almost every startup problem.

It is the only prerequisite. The lab installs nothing else on your computer.

What you should see

A window that works through ten stages. It verifies its own work as it goes, so the last thing it prints before the addresses looks like this:

The end of the setup file's own verification query 1 the whole day of auth events = 280 query 2 the failed logons = 51 query 3 every successful logon = 74 query 4 the alerted account = 3 query 5 the exfiltration = 1 query 6 the process starts = 14 [verify] every number the walkthrough quotes matches the live index.

Those numbers are the answers to this whole investigation. The file has just proved them against the live index, which is why you can trust every count in the rest of this guide. Then it prints:

The last thing the setup file prints The lab is ready. Elasticsearch : http://127.0.0.1:9200 Kibana : http://127.0.0.1:5601 data view "auth" index pattern auth-* data view "network" index pattern network-* Kibana login lab_kibana / LabKibana001 in curl -u lab_kibana:LabKibana001

It also prints the six investigation queries at the end as a reference sheet, so you can compare your work against them afterwards.

What it did for you while you waited

So the output does not frighten you, the file did exactly the jobs that would otherwise be the hard part of this lab:

  • Started two programs — Elasticsearch (the database) first, then Kibana (the website) — and created the throwaway account Kibana runs as.
  • Taught Elasticsearch what each field means. An index template declares “source.ip holds a network address” before any data arrives. Without it Elasticsearch guesses, and guessing quietly breaks your searches.
  • Loaded the log data — 294 documents into auth-* and 126 into network-*.
  • Created your two data views, then read the stored index pattern back to prove it really was written. So when Kibana opens, everything is already there. You do not need to create them yourself.
  • Installed the detection rule and waited for it to fire. The alert you are about to read did not exist until the file did that, and the file does not print ready until the alerts are really there — three of them. If the rule had matched nothing you would have been told so instead of being handed an empty page.

The two data views waiting for you

auth-*auth-*29415

Already started it twice?

Completely safe. The script counts what is already there and skips the import if the numbers match. Your data will not load twice — which matters, because duplicate documents would double every count in the rest of this guide and quietly ruin your findings. If it ever finds a wrong number it refuses to import rather than guess, and tells you to run setup-lab.cmd reset.

What you are looking at

Do this

  1. Look at the Severity column. Every row says critical. Look at Risk Score beside it: 99.
  2. Find the count just above the table, next to Columns. It says 3 alerts. That is three separate events, not one summary.
  3. Read the Reason column on any row. It tells you the records came from a single source address and were for jdoe. Write those two down.
  4. Open one alert. In the first column, called Actions, click the first small icon — the two arrows pointing outwards. That is the next card.
Two different times, and the difference matters

An alert is stamped with the time the rule ran, not the time the event happened, so the log record underneath it happened on 22 September, in the morning. The alerts are new and the events they point at are old. That is why the Alerts page opens on Today and shows three, while Discover shows nothing at all until you set its time range. It is not a fault.

Open one alert on the JSON tab and you will find two clocks on it:

The two timestamps, from one alert@timestamp 2026-09-30T13:00:47.791Z the day YOU ran this kibana.alert.original_time 2026-09-22T10:00:00.000Z the morning of the attack

@timestamp is when Elastic noticed, so it is a different date for every batch and it tells you nothing about the attack. kibana.alert.original_time is when the activity actually happened, and that one never moves — for this lab it is always 22 September 2026.

So: an alert is a claim that something happened; the original time is the evidence for it. Every real SOC works this way, because logs often arrive late and a rule is frequently run against history — and if alerts were dated by the event, today’s real alerts would be buried under a wall of old ones. Which one goes in your report? The original time. Every time you write in this lab, write the time of the activity, never the time the tool noticed it.

What the rule deliberately does not do

It fires on one account name. It does not measure how far apart those addresses are, and it does not measure how little time passed between them. Those two facts are what turn three logons into an incident, and establishing them by hand is the exercise in the next twelve cards.

A real deployment would use a short window, index the geo fields, and alert on the velocity of logons rather than on one account name — because the account name is exactly the thing an attacker changes first.

Lab is running5

One alert, opened

the evidence inside4 min

Click the small two outward arrows in the Actions column of any row. A panel slides in from the right. Three tabs sit across the top: Overview, Table and JSON — the same alert shown three ways. Overview is the readable one.

Three alerts, and they are not the same event three times

Open all three rows and you will find the reason names a different source address each time, at three different times, on the same host, for the same account. That is not one attack repeating itself. That is three separate sign-ins, and the fact that they are three is the whole reason this page is interesting.

Do not start building your argument from the reason string. Treat the alert as a pointer: it has told you the account and the machine, and now you have to prove the rest yourself, in Discover, in order.

The rule behind the three

Worth seeing, because the rule and your own investigation are the same filter.

  1. Close the alert panel with the × at its top right, then open the hamburger menu (☰) top left and choose Security → Rules. Ours is the only rule you have, so it sits on its own.
  2. Click the rule name to open it. Read the Definition panel on the right.
The number on the alert page is a promise, not a hope

Because the rule and the investigation are the same filter, the 3 alerts on the previous card and the Documents (3) you will get from Query 4 later are the same three records. If your alert page said a different number from your query, the rule and the query would be telling different stories and one of them would be wrong — which is worth knowing before you write anything down.

The setup file knows this too. It does not print The lab is ready. until it has read 3 alerts out of the index the Alerts page reads, so if the page were empty you would have been told so instead of being handed an empty screen.

Lab is running6

Open Discover. This screen looks broken. It is not.

one click to fix

You have read the alert. Now put it down and go and prove it, and the tool to do that with is Discover. The setup file opened Kibana on the Alerts page, so Discover is one click away: open the hamburger menu (☰) top left, or use the stack selector in the top bar, and pick Discover.

This card exists because what you are looking at shows no data at all, and that is expected. Let’s read it together, piece by piece.

  • 1 Data view — which pile of logs you are reading. It already says auth-*, which is the one you want. Leave it alone.
  • 2 The wide empty box is the search bar, and every query in this guide is typed here. Its hint text reads Filter your data using KQL syntax.
  • 3 Last 15 minutes — the time picker. This is why you see nothing. The events happened on 22 September 2026, which is not inside the last fifteen minutes.
  • 4 Empty fields  15 on the left is not an error. It means “this data view has 15 fields, but none of them hold data inside the last 15 minutes”.
  • 5 The blue Search entire time range button. Click this next. It is the quickest way to see your data and it is the right first move.
So what is wrong right now?

Exactly one thing: the time range. The data view is right, the search bar is fine, Kibana is healthy. The logs are simply older than the last fifteen minutes.

That is the single most common reason a beginner meets an empty screen. The Search entire time range button fixes it for you. The next card after that shows you how to do the same thing by hand, so you can pin an exact window rather than “everything”.

Watch the sidebar change as you work

Right now the sidebar lists Available fields 0, Empty fields 15 and Meta fields 4, and nothing else. As you start clicking fields, Kibana quietly adds a Popular fields group at the top, listing the ones you have used.

That is normal and harmless — it has no effect on your results. It simply means this lab started clean. Read Available fields for the full list and ignore the rest.

Pick a pile7

Check which pile of logs you are reading

which logs?2 min

Discover needs to be told which pile of logs to read. You have two, and only one of them is where this investigation starts.

Do this

  1. Find the dropdown on the far left of the search bar — the control immediately right of the words Data view.
  2. Click it. This is what opens — a short list, and nothing else changes.
  3. Check the list contains auth-* and network-*, and that auth-* is the one with the tick beside it. If it already is, there is nothing to do — move straight on.
What the two data views are
Data viewHoldsDocumentsFields
auth-*Logons, logoffs, failures, lockouts, privilege assignments and program starts29415
network-*Connections between machines, with ports, protocols and byte counts12616

The * is a wildcard meaning “anything starting with auth”, so one entry covers every day of auth logs. We start with auth-* because the alert is about logons, and we switch to network-* in card 17.

Why this matters more than it looks

A data view is a bookmark. It tells Kibana which pile of documents to read and which field holds the time. Pick the wrong one and a perfectly good query returns nothing at all, because the documents it is looking for are not in that pile.

So whenever a query returns zero results, check these three things in this order: the data view, then the time range, then the query itself. Nine times out of ten it is one of the first two, never the third.

If the list is empty, or the sidebar says “no available fields” even after you pick one

Then the data views were not created properly. Do not fight it — run setup-lab.cmd again. It is safe to run twice, it reloads nothing, and it now verifies each data view and tells you if anything is wrong instead of printing a hopeful message.

Be precise8

Set the time range, and read the times carefully

pin an exact window4 min

Your data is loaded and the right data view is selected. The screen is still empty for one reason only, and this card fixes it for good.

The easy way, if you would rather not fight with dates

Go back to card 7 and click Search entire time range. All of this lab’s data falls inside one day, so that button selects exactly the window you want, and every count in this guide matches. The rest of this card is for when you want to pin the window yourself — which is what a real analyst does.

Do this the exact way

  1. Click the time picker, the control that currently reads Last 15 minutes. A panel opens.
  2. It has three tabs across the top, and the order is Absolute, Relative, Now. Absolute is already the one selected, which is what you want.
  3. Use the September and 2026 dropdowns if they are not already on the right month, then click 22 in the calendar.
  4. A Start date row appears at the bottom with a value in it. Set it to Sep 22, 2026 @ 00:00:00.000.
  5. An End date row appears. Set it to Sep 22, 2026 @ 23:59:59.999. The .999 matters: leave it out and you lose the last fraction of a second.
  6. Click Update — or just click outside the panel, which applies it too.
What you should see — the whole lab opens up

The time button now reads a range instead of a vague “last 15 minutes”, and:

  • The Documents tab reads Documents (294) — your first real result. The number lives inside the tab name, which is where you will look for it from now on.
  • The blue histogram appears with bars across the day. That is your instant visual proof you are looking at the right day.
  • The sidebar fills in: Available fields 15 replaces Empty fields 15, and all fifteen field names appear.
The one thing that will look “wrong”: Kibana prints times in your timezone

This trips up almost everyone, so read it before you go further.

The timestamps in this lab are stored in UTC. But the @timestamp column, the histogram axis, and the dates inside a document all follow your computer’s timezone, and no setting anywhere in Kibana changes that. If your machine is 8 hours ahead of UTC, an event stored at 10:00:00 appears in your table as 18:00:00.

You may also notice the range you just pinned shows up as 08:00:00.000 – 07:59:59.999 rather than 00:00:00.000 – 23:59:59.999. That is the same window, and your row counts will be identical. It is not a mistake and there is nothing to fix.

So which is right? Both, and it does not matter. Here is the rule that keeps you out of trouble:

  • Read the clock times off your own screen and write down what you see. Your timeline will be internally consistent, which is all a timeline needs.
  • Trust the gaps, not the absolute numbers. Every conclusion in this guide is about how far apart things are, and a timezone shift moves every time by the same amount. The gaps survive any timezone on earth.
  • One place shows the raw stored value. Open a single logon, switch the panel from Table to JSON, and the original ISO string is right there with its Z. Card 16 shows you. That one form never shifts.
Remember this one, and it will save you hours

An empty screen in Kibana is almost never a broken query. It is almost always the time range or the data view. Check those two first, every time.

And beware: if you ever press F5 to reload, the time picker goes back to Last 15 minutes and your records disappear again. It is not deleted — just re-pin the range and it comes straight back.

Query 1 of 89

Query 1 — the whole day’s authentication trail

1 of 8 queries2 min
Goal

Get a control number. Before you can say something is unusual you need to know what normal looks like, and how much of it there is.

Do this

  1. Click in the search bar and select whatever is in it, then paste this in its place. Do not delete the data view or the time range — only the search text.
  2. Press Enter.
Query 1 · data view auth-* · copy then pasteevent.category: authentication
Finding

The Documents tab reads Documents (280). Out of 294 documents in this pile, 280 are authentication events and the other 14 are program starts. Write 280 down — it is the denominator for every comparison that follows.

Why start here

Because “impossible travel” means nothing without a denominator. If the alerted account had made three logons out of three, that would be ordinary. Three out of 280, in a different pattern, is not. Analysts call this a control number, and it is the cheapest possible way to stop yourself over-reacting to a scary looking count in the next five minutes.

Next

The most obvious next move for a login alert is to look at failed logins. Do that. It will not work, and that is the point of the next card.

Query 2 of 810

Query 2 — 51 failed logons, and why that is a dead end

dead end4 min
Goal

Test the most obvious hypothesis: an overnight alert about sign-ins often means somebody was hammering a password. Look at the failures and see.

Do this

  1. Replace the search text with the query below and press Enter.
  2. In the left sidebar, click the field called user.name to expand it. Click the field name itself — a small panel opens underneath it with a Top values list.
Query 2 · data view auth-* · copy then pasteevent.code: 4625
Finding

Documents (51) — fifty-one failed logons. That sounds alarming. And when you expand user.name the sidebar lists exactly five accounts:

AccountShare of the 51 failures
svega25.5%
kpatel21.6%
mchen21.6%
asmith19.6%
rneuman11.8%

The account in the alert is not on that list. The alerted account jdoe has zero failed logons in the entire day.

This is a dead end, and saying so out loud is the skill

Fifty-one failed logons is ordinary background noise for a company with six accounts and a day of work in it. It is spread across five different people, and the person the alert is about never failed once. There is nothing here for you to escalate.

An analyst who stopped here would have written a confident report about a brute-force attack that never happened. The number was big; the pattern was absent. Big numbers on their own are not evidence — that sentence is worth more than the query you just ran.

Next

Impossible travel is about successes, not failures. A failed attempt never got in. Widen the filter to successful logons and the account count will finally include the right person.

Query 3 of 811

Query 3 — 74 successes. Still not evidence.

not yet3 min
Goal

Drop the failures and keep only logons that actually succeeded. This is the population the alert is really about.

Do this

  1. Replace the search text with the query below and press Enter. It has two clauses joined by and — keep both, and keep the quotation marks.
Query 3 · data view auth-* · copy then pasteevent.code: 4624 and event.outcome: "success"
  • 1 event.code: 4624 — the Windows code for “an account was successfully logged on”.
  • 2 event.outcome: "success" — keep only the ones that worked. The quotation marks matter: success without them is a different search.
  • 3 The word and between them means both must be true. That is how you narrow a search down in this language.
Finding

Documents (74) successful logons for the whole company. Six accounts share them. One of them is the account in the alert, with 3 of the 74 — and you are about to go and look at exactly those three.

Careful: 74 is not the answer either

It is tempting to stop here, because 74 is a lot and the account is in there somewhere. But “one account made three logons out of seventy-four” is a statement about volume, and volume is not what the alert is about. The alert is about where those logons came from.

Next

Add the third clause: the account named in the alert. This is the query the alert actually wanted you to run.

Query 4 of 812

Query 4 — three logons, and the case starts to look wrong

breakthrough4 min
Goal

Isolate every successful logon for the account named in the alert, and nothing else. Three rows is a small enough result set to read completely.

Do this

  1. Replace the search text with the query below and press Enter.
  2. The search bar now holds all three clauses. Keep them — you will reuse this exact query later.
Query 4 · data view auth-* · copy then pasteevent.code: 4624 and event.outcome: "success" and user.name: "jdoe"
  • 1 Documents (3). The number lives inside the tab name. Write 3 down.
  • 2 Columns 6 on the right. The chart is off and Columns 6 is on, because this picture is zoomed in on the rows. To see source.ip and host.name as columns of their own, click Columns 6 and add them — or just read them out of the expanded Summary column, which already contains everything.
  • 3 The green success badge and 4,624 in every row. All three really did get in. That is what makes them interesting.
  • 4 The yellow boxes are the three values you must now read off your own screen: the time, the source address and the machine, once each. Write all three down now, before moving on.
Finding

Three successful logons, and they are the only three in the entire dataset for this account. Nothing else in the day involves jdoe at all — no failures, no lockouts, no program starts. Whatever happened, it happened in these three rows.

Why three rows is progress and not the answer

Because three rows on their own prove nothing. What makes them a finding is the shape of them, and there are two things left to check: how many different places they came from, and how much time passed. Do the first one now.

Next

Do not read the timestamps yet. First count the places, because that is the part of the claim that cannot be argued with.

Query 5 of 813

Query 5 — how many different places?

the shape5 min
Goal

Count the distinct source addresses behind those three logons. Same query as before — you are only changing how the screen is arranged.

Do this

  1. Change nothing about the query. It still reads event.code: 4624 and event.outcome: "success" and user.name: "jdoe" and the tab still says Documents (3).
  2. In the left sidebar, click the field source.ip to expand it. A panel opens with a Top values list.
  3. Count the entries in that list. Every entry is a different address.
  4. Write the three addresses down, one per row, in the order they appear in the table — not in the order the sidebar happens to sort them.
Finding

Three distinct source addresses, one logon each, 33.3% apiece. Not one address used three times — three addresses used once each. And the address on every row of the results table is not an internal 10.0.4.x address, so all three are external: out on the internet, somewhere else in the world.

One account, successfully authenticated, from three different external places. Write the three addresses in your notes now.

A second, tidier way to count them — the Field statistics tab

Next to Documents (3) there is a tab called Field statistics. It is a tab on the same bar, not a section further down. Click it and you get one row per field with a Distinct values column:

FieldDocumentsDistinct valuesWhat it says
event.code3 (100%)11 value (4624) — all three are the same kind of event
event.outcome3 (100%)11 category — all three succeeded
user.name3 (100%)11 category — one account
host.name3 (100%)11 category — one machine, and it is the same machine every time
source.ip3 (100%)33 categories — three different places

Read the last two rows together. One machine, three places. The account did not move between computers — something out there kept logging in to the same computer from three directions. The machine it logged in to is on your screen in the host.name column; read it off and write it down, because you need it in card 17.

Next

Before you celebrate: check that “three external addresses” is actually unusual here. One card left of dead, and it is the more important of the two.

Query 6 of 814

Query 6 — “six external addresses” is a trap

dead end4 min
Goal

Challenge your own finding. “Three external addresses” is only a finding if three external addresses is not normal here. Go and check.

Do this

  1. Go back one card to Query 3’s search text (event.code: 4624 and event.outcome: "success", no account clause) and run it. You should get Documents (74) again.
  2. Expand source.ip in the left sidebar and read the whole Top values list.
  3. Count how many of the addresses are external (anything not starting 10.0.4.).
  4. Now find out who else is using those addresses. Click any one of them in the sidebar list and look at what the panel underneath says.
Query 6 · data view auth-* · this is Query 3 again, deliberatelyevent.code: 4624 and event.outcome: "success"
Here is the trap, and it is a good one

You can read this list and say: “six external addresses appear in this company’s successful logins today. Six! That must be an attack.” It is exactly the wrong conclusion, and here is why.

Look at the percentages. Three of those external addresses are used ten to twelve times each by the other five accounts, spread right across the working day. Those are your office’s normal outbound addresses — a proxy or a VPN concentrator that everybody leaves through. The other three are used once each, by one account, inside a few minutes.

External addressLogonsShareWho used itVerdict
192.0.2.101216.2%all five other accounts, all dayordinary
203.0.113.91114.9%four other accounts, all dayordinary
198.51.100.421013.5%four other accounts, all dayordinary
 three addresses 1 each1.4% eachthe alerted account onlythe finding

The rare thing is not “an external address”. The rare thing is an external address used exactly once, by exactly one person, while every colleague comes in through the same three doors.

The habit this card is really teaching

Before you escalate a number, ask “compared to what?” A count on its own has no meaning. Six external addresses means nothing until you know that five other people use three of them all day. Always look at the whole list and the percentages, not just at the thing that worried you — and remember that the rarest entries in a list are usually the interesting ones, not the biggest.

Next

Put the account clause back and finally look at the clock. One address used once is suggestive. Three of them inside a few minutes is the thing the alert is named after.

Query 7 of 815

Query 7 — how long did it take?

the verdict turns on this5 min
Goal

Turn three places into a distance. Impossible travel is not about being in three places; it is about being in three places in no time at all.

Do this

  1. Put the account clause back if you removed it, so the tab reads Documents (3) again.
  2. Look at the @timestamp column down the left of the three rows. Write down all three times exactly as your screen shows them.
  3. Subtract. First gap: time 2 minus time 1. Second gap: time 3 minus time 2. Total: time 3 minus time 1.
  4. To see the same event in UTC — the form that never shifts — click the two-diagonal-arrow expander immediately left of the timestamp on the first row, then switch the panel from Table to JSON.
Do not click the row

Clicking anywhere on a row does nothing. The control that opens a document is the small two-diagonal-arrow button immediately to the left of the timestamp. The square box further left is a select checkbox — ticking it selects the row and tells you nothing.

Write these four values down now, from your own screen
1st logon — time
1st logon — source address
2nd logon — time
2nd logon — source address
3rd logon — time
3rd logon — source address
The machine all three used
Finding

Your two gaps and your total should come to:

  • First gap: 6 minutes.
  • Second gap: 8 minutes.
  • Total, first logon to last: 14 minutes.

So: one account, three successful logons, from three different external addresses, to the same machine, inside fourteen minutes. If your machine is 8 hours ahead of UTC the three times read 8 hours later — the gaps are identical, and the gaps are the finding.

Why fourteen minutes settles it

Because the three addresses are not merely different, they are in different countries — different address blocks, thousands of kilometres apart. Nobody flies, takes a train and clears a border in six minutes, three times in a row, and lands on the same keyboard each time.

There are only two explanations left, and both are bad:

  • The credentials were stolen and are being used by more than one party (this is what the evidence supports), or
  • The account is shared between people in different places, which is a policy problem that still needs a response and still needs this report.

Either way the alert is a true positive. But “impossible travel” on its own is an account-compromise finding, not a finished investigation. A stolen account is worth far more to an attacker than a password, and the next question is: what did they take?

Next

Switch to the network-* pile and look for something leaving the machine you just wrote down.

Query 8 of 816

Query 8 — did data leave the building?

the payoff6 min
Goal

Turn a compromised account into a data breach. Find the connection that moved far more data than anything else on the network, and see where it went.

Do this

  1. Change the Data view dropdown from auth-* to network-*. The whole screen reloads and the tab goes back to Documents (0) while it works.
  2. Type the query below and press Enter.
  3. Add the columns that matter: click Columns on the right of the tab bar and add network.bytes, source.ip, destination.ip and destination.port.
  4. Sort by size: click the network.bytes column heading once. A small down arrow appears beside the name and the biggest value is now the top row.
Query 8 · data view network-* · copy then pastenetwork.protocol: "https"
Finding

Documents (15) encrypted connections that day. Sorted largest first, the top row is covered up — and the second row is 65,030 bytes. The row above it moves roughly 740 times more than anything else in the entire dataset: about 46 megabytes in a single connection, where ordinary traffic here is measured in tens of kilobytes.

Read that top row and you have the last piece:

The top row — fill this in from your own screen
When
Bytes moved
Left which machine (IP)
Went to which address
Destination port

Then make the check that turns two findings into one:

  • The source is the machine you wrote down on card 16 — the same workstation all three logons went to.
  • The destination is one of the three external addresses you wrote down on card 14. One of them. Not a new one. Check this yourself, and if it does not match, say so in the report rather than assuming.
  • The time is under six minutes after the last logon.
One lead that looks promising and is not

By now you are hunting for a program the attacker ran — the classic smoking gun. The auth-* pile really does contain program starts:

The lead · data view auth-* · copy then pasteevent.code: 4688

You cannot use the answer. Here is why, and it is worth knowing because it is true of a great many real investigations: not one of those 14 records carries a source.ip field at all. The nearest program start on the compromised machine is more than an hour after the last logon, and there is nothing in the data that connects a process to the session that preceded it.

So write “no process-level evidence is available in this telemetry” in your report. That sentence is worth more than a guess. Inventing a process name is how reports become fiction.

Next

You have everything. Build the timeline, then write the report.

Put it together17

Build the timeline

oldest first5 min

Open a text file or a piece of paper. List your four events oldest first, with the value you read off your own screen. The result should be a four-line sequence that reads like a story with a beginning and an end.

Fill this in — four rows, oldest at the top

Your timeline
EventTime, as your screen showed it
Successful logon, first external address
Successful logon, second external address
Successful logon, third external address
Large outbound transfer to one of those addresses
What a good timeline looks like

Four lines, all inside a twenty-minute window, reading in this order: three sign-ins from three far-apart places, then a single enormous upload to one of those same places. The shape matters more than the digits — that window is itself evidence, and it is far easier to see in a list than scattered across a search screen.

If your four times do not fit inside about twenty minutes, you have probably mixed up the stored UTC times with the displayed local times. Go back to card 9.

Why a timeline and not just a list of findings

Because a timeline is an argument. Separate findings are just facts: “three logons”, “one big transfer”. Laid out in order they become cause and effect — the logons came first, the transfer followed, and the transfer went somewhere the logons came from. That is what turns a pile of queries into a finding, and it is what makes the difference between a report that gets escalated and one that gets closed.

Two things to leave out, deliberately

Do not put the 51 failed logons or the 6 external addresses in the timeline. They are not part of this incident — they are the ordinary background against which it stands out. A timeline is a list of things that mattered. Padding it with irrelevant numbers is how a good report gets ignored.

Write18

Write the report, then export it

five sections15 min

Five sections, in this order. Type them in the boxes below as you go — the EXPORT MY SUBMISSION button at the bottom of this card builds a PDF report out of exactly what is in them, and nothing else. Write the Summary last: once you know the shape of the thing, the summary writes itself.

Nothing on this card is an answer. There is deliberately no worked example, no sample summary and no verdict written out for you — every figure your report needs is one you read off your own screen, and the only source of them is the investigation you just did. The boxes say what a section has to contain, and that is all.

These two are printed at the top of the exported file. Nothing here is ever filled in for you, and both stay empty until you type into them.

1. Summary

Two to four sentences: what happened, who was affected, and the verdict in one line. Your instructor reads this and nothing else.

What it has to contain Four things, in four sentences at most: what happened, in one sentence and in plain words; who or what was affected, naming the account and the host; the pattern that makes it more than a curiosity, in one sentence; and the verdict, as the two words themselves. Your instructor reads this and nothing else, so if a reader who has never seen this lab cannot follow it, it is not finished.

No numbers yet Do not write the count, the addresses, the window or the byte total in the summary — or if you do, write them only because you have already verified them on your own screen. Every figure in this report has to come from your screen, not from a number you half-remember.

2. Timeline

Your four rows from the last card, oldest first, with the exact values you read off your own screen.

What it has to contain A two-column table — Time and Event — one row per event you recorded on the previous card, oldest first. Times exactly as your screen showed them, and one line under the table saying which timezone those times are displayed in, because they are not UTC. Nothing else in the report needs a timestamp, so this is the only place a reader can check your sequence.

3. Evidence

Each query you ran, and the specific thing it proved. One line each.

What it has to contain One line per query, in the form the query → the specific thing it proved. Not “I searched for logons” — that is not evidence, that is a keystroke. A line is only evidence if it could be checked by someone else: the query, the number that came back, and the conclusion you drew from that number.

Include the dead ends — in one line each Every query you ran that proved nothing is still evidence, and saying so is worth marks. A report that only lists its hits is indistinguishable from a report written by someone who got lucky. One line per dead end: what you expected, what you actually found, and why it ruled the hypothesis out.

Include the lead you could not follow If a query could not be taken further, write that down as a limitation. One sentence saying what you tried and what the data would not let you conclude is stronger than a confident guess, and it is what a real analyst does.

4. Verdict

True positive or false positive, and the chain in one paragraph.

What it has to contain The two words true positive or false positive, stated outright and in capitals on their own line — not implied, and not buried at the end of a paragraph. Then, one paragraph, the chain: each finding in the order it happened, and the reasoning that connects them. “A happened, then B, and A causes B” is a chain. Two unrelated facts in a row is a list.

Then say what rules the other verdict out Name the pattern you would have expected if this were benign, and say why it is not present. That is what turns a verdict into a judgement. A verdict with nothing ruling out the alternative is a guess with a full stop.

5. Recommendations

Short, concrete, actionable. Four or five of them. Write your own — there is deliberately no list of answers on this card.

Shape of the recommendationWhy it is written that way
Something you must do today, naming the account or host involvedan action with no name and no deadline is a wish
Something that stops the next occurrence of this exact patterna control that only works because you are watching
Something that finds out how bad it was — scope, and who was affectedcontainment without scope leaves the worst part unknown
Something that makes this visible earlier next timethe cheapest fix is the alert that did not exist yet

The report is the deliverable, not the queries

Nobody is grading how many searches you ran. They are grading whether the report names the account, the count, the number of places, the window, and the transfer, and whether the verdict follows from them. If any of those five is missing, the report does not get escalated no matter how good the rest of it is.

Write the numbers you read off your screen, not the numbers you half-remember. If they disagree with what the setup file verified, something is wrong and the troubleshooting card will tell you how to find out what.

Export it

The button builds the file for you out of what you typed: your name and batch at the top, then your five written sections, each under the label you typed it against. Anything you left blank is written in as [not answered] rather than quietly dropped, so a hole cannot turn into a tidy-looking submission. The PDF lands in your Downloads folder; nothing is uploaded and no internet connection is needed.

Your finished submission

Before you submit, check all eight

If any of these is no, it is not finished:

  • Your name and batch at the top of this card are filled in.
  • Every one of the five boxes has something in it — not a placeholder, your own words.
  • Your summary would still make sense to someone who has never heard of Windows logon codes.
  • Your timeline is in order and every line has a time on it.
  • Your evidence names the query, the number and the conclusion for each.
  • Your verdict is one of the two words, stated outright, not implied.
  • Your recommendations would survive being read by someone who has to pay for them.
  • You have pressed EXPORT MY SUBMISSION, opened the PDF, and handed in the file.
Wrap up19

Take the lab apart

one file

The lab is two containers and one volume. One file removes all three, and it will ask you first.

Do this

  1. Close the browser tab with Kibana in it.
  2. In the lab folder, run the teardown file for your system: on Windows, double-click teardown.cmd; on macOS or Linux, run ./teardown.sh in a terminal in that folder (or bash teardown.sh).
  3. It lists exactly what it is about to delete — the two containers named after this folder, the volume that holds the data and the alert, the generated compose file and its own scratch folder — and asks you to confirm (Y or N on Windows, y or n on macOS and Linux). Read the list, then say yes.
  4. It finishes by verifying the removal and telling you what it kept. Confirm from its closing summary that the volume is gone.
What it will not do
  • It does not remove any Docker image. The two large Elastic images stay on your machine so the next setup takes seconds instead of minutes.
  • It does not run docker system prune and does not touch any other container, volume or project on your machine. Every name it deletes is derived from this folder’s name, so a second scenario lab sitting alongside this one is completely unaffected.
  • It is safe to run twice. The second time it says there is nothing to remove and stops.
If you want to keep the data instead

Do nothing, or run docker compose -f docker-compose.yml stop. That stops the two containers and leaves everything on disk, so the next setup-lab.cmd or ./setup-lab.sh picks up exactly where you left off — and neither will re-import anything. Only run the teardown file when you are finished with the scenario for good.

If you want the answers gone with it

The teardown file deletes the containers and the volume, which is where every document and the alert live. After it finishes, none of it exists on this machine. The files in this folder — the logs, the templates, rule.json, this guide — are all still there, and the teardown script has never touched anything outside the names it derived from this folder’s name.

Reference20

If something goes wrong

reference, not a step

Not part of the main path — come here when you are stuck. These are the four things that actually happen, in the order they happen.

1. The screen is empty. Every query returns nothing.

Almost always the time range or the data view, in that order. Look at the time picker on the right of the search bar. If it says anything vaguer than your start and end times — Last 15 minutes, or a bare entire time range — that is the cause. Re-pin Absolute, Sep 22 2026 00:00:00.000 to 23:59:59.999. Then check the Data view dropdown on the left says auth-*.

Pressing F5 resets the time picker to Last 15 minutes and your records vanish again. Nothing is lost — re-pin the range.

2. The sidebar says “0 available fields” even after you pick a data view

Same cause, or the data was never loaded. If the time range is right and it still shows nothing, run setup-lab.cmd again — it is safe, it reloads nothing, and it verifies each data view and tells you if one is broken. If it reports a wrong document count, follow what it says: setup-lab.cmd reset.

3. The setup file says Docker is not installed, or not running

Open Docker Desktop (Windows or macOS) or start the Docker service (Linux) and wait until it says it is running, then run the file again. This one check fixes almost every startup problem, and it is the reason the lab is a single file rather than a list of instructions.

On macOS and Linux, if the file says permission denied, run bash setup-lab.sh instead of ./setup-lab.sh. That always works.

4. You clicked “Try ES|QL” and everything looks different

That button in the top bar switches Discover into a different query language. The button itself changes to Switch to classic, the Data view control disappears, and the empty screen no longer offers a Search entire time range button — so it can look as though your data has gone.

Nothing is wrong and nothing is lost. Click Switch to classic and you are back exactly where you were. This guide only ever uses the KQL search bar.

If the Alerts page is the empty one

Same cause, different page. An alert is stamped with the time the rule ran, not the time the event happened, so the Alerts page opens on Today while the log data is from 22 September 2026. Set its time picker to Last 24 hours or 1 day and the three come back. The alert cards explain the two timestamps, because this one catches everyone out at least once.

If they are still missing, the rule genuinely did not fire. Run the setup file again: it is idempotent, it leaves the existing rule alone, and it refuses to print ready until it has read all three alerts out of the index the Alerts page reads — so it will either fix it, or tell you exactly why it could not.

If you never got a sign-in screen, and did not expect one

This lab’s Kibana has security switched on, so it asks who you are once. The account is lab_kibana and the password is LabKibana001. They are throwaway lab credentials that protect nothing, and the setup file prints them again in its closing summary.

One thing that is not an error

The Popular fields group in the sidebar. Kibana creates it from fields you have already clicked, and it can reappear after a reload. It has no effect on your results. Look at Available fields instead, and ignore it.

If a count still does not match

Work through it in this order and stop at the first that applies: the data view, then the time range, then the query text character by character — including the quotation marks around "success" and around "https". A missing pair of quotation marks is the single most common reason a correct-looking query returns a different number.
